claims.text: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles can be synthesized.
The initial nanoparticles have random cation distributions.
An oxygen-lean or vacuum synthesis atmosphere produces a higher oxygen-vacancy density than an ambient oxidizing atmosphere.
Catalytic service conditions relevant to these nanoparticles span 773–1173 K.
Thermoelectric service conditions relevant to these nanoparticles span 473–1923 K.
Engineered oxygen vacancies create a flexible oxygen sublattice.
A vacancy-containing oxygen sublattice accommodates local lattice strain.
Increased oxygen-vacancy formation accommodates thermally induced lattice stress.
Increased oxygen-vacancy formation suppresses elemental diffusion.
Suppression of elemental diffusion limits phase segregation.
Oxygen-vacancy buffering limits chemical-ordering changes that would destabilize the solid solution.
Oxygen-vacancy-rich nanoparticles will retain their near-equiatomic solid-solution phase better during high-temperature service.
Oxygen-lean synthesis will reduce phase segregation relative to ambient-atmosphere synthesis.
Oxygen-lean synthesis will improve retention of near-equiatomic elemental homogeneity relative to ambient-atmosphere synthesis.
Oxygen-lean synthesis will produce superior catalytic performance relative to ambient-atmosphere synthesis.
Oxygen-lean synthesis will produce superior thermoelectric performance relative to ambient-atmosphere synthesis.
The proposed mechanism requires an oxygen sublattice capable of accommodating vacancies.
The effect will be diminished in materials lacking protective oxide layers or vacancy-related defect chemistry.

contradictions.description: The initial material class includes metallic high-entropy alloys, but the proposed oxygen-vacancy mechanism requires an oxygen sublattice. The boundary narrows applicability to oxygen-containing systems, leaving the hypothesis inapplicable to unoxidized metallic HEA nanoparticles despite their inclusion in the initial state.
